newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: GOVT EXPECTS LEAD LEVELS IN BROKEN HILL BABIES TO IMPROVE
The New South Wales government says its expecting a gradual improvement in lead levels in children in Broken Hill.
A new study has found lead levels in newborn babies in Broken Hill to be much higher than expected.
And a study says the blood lead levels of infants in the New South Wales mining city increases three-fold in their first six months of life.
A spokesman for the Health Department says A$10 million was committed last year to fund a five-year program to clean up the Broken Hill environment.
This is expected to result in a gradual improvement in blood lead levels.
LATEST VICTORIAN SALMONELLA SCARE STARTED IN FEBRUARY
Victoria's Department of Human Services says the salmonella outbreak which has closed a supermaket deli started in February, but the department was only able to interview the victims yesterday.

Department spokesman Malcolm Elder says none of those affected required hospital treatment. Safeway stores closed the deli at an outlet at Frankston after consultation with the department, which traced four of the five cases involving processed meat products there.
The deli will remain closed until the inquiries are completed.
TULLAMARINE AIRPORT WINS INTERNATIONAL RECOGNITION
A global survey of airports has named Melbourne airport the third best in the world.
The International Air Transport Association study of 50,000 passengers ranks Melbourne airport behind only Changi in Singapore and Manchester in the UK.
Tullamarine was Australia's best airport in last year's survey, when it was ranked seventh among the world's airports.
It was rated world's best for its restaurant and eating facilities.
IMPORTED NURSES WILL FILL IMMEDIATE SHORTAGE
The Immigration Department says nurses recruited overseas by the Northern Territory will fill an immediate shortage, while Australian nurses gain further skills.
The Northern Territory's Health Services has applied to the Federal Government to become a business migration sponsor.
The department acknowledges the Territory has trouble recruiting specialist nurses because of its isolation and says there is a nationwide shortage of nurses in specialist areas.

The Territory Health Services says it wants to bring in nurses from Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom for up to two years and is also considering using the Regional Sponsored Migration Scheme.
PHARMACIES SCORE POOR MARKS IN ASTHMA SURVEY
A national survey of 200 pharmacies by the Consumers' Association has found nearly half failed when giving advice on asthma medication.
Choice says staff in some pharmacies were found to be breaking the law by selling asthma puffers without advice from pharmacists.
The association's Gail Kennedy says fewer than a third of pharmacies visited were rated good or excellent, while almost half were poor or negligent.
Ms Kennedy says the results are disturbing, given Australia's high incidence of asthma.
Results were better in New South Wales and the ACT where pharmacies are required to issue or see an asthma card. Ms Kennedy says the card should be introduced across the country.
QLD POLICE UNION PRESIDENT DEFENDS POLICE VIOLENCE

The president of the Queensland Police Union, Gary Wilkinson, has defended police filmed punching and kicking a group of Aborigines while making arrests outside a nightclub in the south-east Queensland city of Ipswich.
Mr Wilkinson says the group put up a a lot of resistance and police have a responsibility to use whatever force is necessary to subdue violence, for the protection of themselves and the public.
Mr Wilkinson has accused the Ipswich Aboriginal Legal Service and the Civil Liberties Council of exaggerating the story behind the two-week-old video in their protests against the police action.
Meanwhile, an Aboriginal youth worker in Ipswich says police are do not have a good reputation because they are not sitting down to talk with community groups.
HOUSEHOLDERS COULD CUT GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS
The Consumers' Association says households can save up to A$1,000 per year by changing the way they consume energy.
The survey of over one-thousand-500 Australian homes shows better energy habits can save money and the environment.
Choice says households are responsible for almost one-fifth of greenhouse gas emissions.
But the association says energy saving tips don't have to mean compromising comfort and convenience.
